centre_guide.text: Welcome to the Causeway! Most of the columns have six sides. Some have four, five, seven, even eight. There are no sides on the sea. We've checked.
The tallest columns are about 12 metres high. They're basalt, so they won't be moved. Visitors, on the other hand, move quite a lot.

geologist.text: Sixty million years ago this was lava. Now it's a staircase. If that doesn't make you feel small, I'll draw you a diagram.
The columns formed as the lava cooled and shrank. It cracked in a regular pattern, like drying mud. The hexagon wins because it uses the least crack for the most room.

visitor.text: I wished on the Wishing Chair. I wished for a cup of tea. I got a coach party, but the tea followed.
Everyone talks about Fionn. Nobody asks about his wife, who was the cleverest person in the legend. She baked a griddle into a loaf and fed it to the rival.

local_man.text: I've lived beside the Causeway sixty years. The rocks haven't changed. I have.
They say a pony the colour of sea foam gallops the waves off here in the mist. Manannán's horse, the old ones called it. Mind you, the old ones also said the tide could be bribed.

then.text: The surf at the foot of the stones is quiet. A line of foam runs along the rock in the shape of a hoofprint, and then the tide takes it.

else.text: The pale horse stands in the shallows, steady as a statue, waves breaking against her knees. She watches you the way the sea watches a harbour wall.
Ná bí buartha. Don't be anxious. I carried a god over a thousand miles of grey water. I can carry a walker a few fields. If you are worth the crossing.

then.text: The horse steps out of the surf and falls in beside you, the sea running off her coat in silver threads. The gulls go silent, as if a bishop had walked in.

else.text: Manannán's Horse folds into the surf and is gone, leaving only a long curl of foam along the rocks. She will be back on the next high tide, if you want to try again.
Sea mist rolls over the far stack and the shape in it is only foam. Perhaps.

then.text: I am not here. This is a mirage. The lease was never signed.

else.text: On the flat ground above the stones stands a very large white marquee. Its banner reads: THE GIANT'S CAUSEWAY EXPERIENCE, PREMIUM TIER.
Beneath it, in a crimson silk scarf that has never once been rained on, Lord Ambrose Vane directs a survey with a gold pencil and the air of a man who owns the weather.
Do mind the lease, walker. It's an excellent lease. It was signed by me, witnessed by me, and notarised by a gentleman who is entirely theoretical.
Ah. The walker. I wondered when I'd have the pleasure. I use the word loosely.
Forty thousand columns, all perfectly sized for a gift shop floor. Do you know what I'd give to own this?
No. Of course you don't. Very well, a little sport. I expect to lose; one always does, against the earnest.
A breeze comes in off the sea, cool and salt and smelling of rain that hasn't started yet. The gulls on the marquee roof, who were arguing, stop.
The sea does not rise so much as arrive. It draws back from the foot of the stones in one long breath, and then it comes in again with something inside it.

Out of the surf rears a pale horse, made of sea-foam and light, with a mane like breaking waves and hooves that ring on the water like a bell. Manannán's Horse. In the old stories it ran over land and sea alike without wetting a hoof.
I say. That is. That's a rather unlicensed animal.
The horse tosses its head. One wave, polite and enormous, lifts the marquee off its pegs, sets it down in a rock pool upside down, and hangs the banner neatly on a basalt column. The gulls cheer.
That is a breach of the lease. I should like it recorded that this was an act of God. Several of them, I suspect, working in concert.
Fine. FINE. The Causeway may keep its columns. We'll meet at the Moot, walker. Everyone does, in the end. Bring a coat.

He squelches off along the cliff path, gold pencil held high, his crimson scarf wrung out like a dishcloth. Behind him, the horse shakes out its mane and looks straight at you. It isn't leaving. It's waiting to be asked.

then.text: Me? I sell keyrings! Look at them! They're round! Does that look like a hexagon to you?
Tuesday I was unloading two hundred stones from Ballymoney. My back's still not forgiven me. Ask anyone. Well, don't ask the seagulls, they're no use.

else.text: Genuine Causeway stones, three pound! Well. Genuine Ballymoney stones. It's the same sea, give or take a county.

then.text: Hilary Gault, retired lecturer, enthusiast. Yes, I measured the Stone of Fionn last week. With a tape. No more than that. Basalt cools and shrinks, and the cracks meet at about 120 degrees, so you get six sides. Lovely.
On Tuesday night I was at Coleraine library paying a 40p fine. I have the slip. I keep all my slips. It is a failing.

else.text: Columnar jointing: the crack pattern you get when something cools evenly. Sorry. I do go on.

landsky_atlantic.text: {greeting} I study volcanoes, and this is one of my favourites, because it's finished. Sixty million years ago the crust tore between Europe and Greenland, the Atlantic began to open, and the lava poured up through the tear.

The same flood of basalt made Mull and Skye and Staffa over the water. Fingal's Cave has the same columns, because it's the same rock cooling the same way. The red band in the cliffs is old soil, a warm wet pause between two flows: proper tropical weathering, in Antrim.

options: Cooling lava shrinks and cracks at even angles
Giants carved them for the road
The sea rolled them round, then square

then.text: Spot on. Lava cools from the top down and shrinks. Cracks meet at about 120 degrees because that uses the least cracking for the most relief, and 120 three times round is a hexagon. The slower it cools, the bigger the columns.

else.text: Good story, wrong rock. Lava cools and shrinks, and the cracks meet at about 120 degrees, which is the cheapest way to split: three of those round a point and you've a hexagon. Drying mud does the same, smaller.

landsky_atlantic.text: The Earth's still doing it. The mid-Atlantic ridge is pulling Europe and America apart by about as much as your fingernails grow each year. Iceland sits right on the seam, and it's a lot less finished than this.
